title: carboxy-endcapped conductive polypyrrole: biomimetic conducting polymer for cell scaffolds and electrodes
display_name: Carboxy-Endcapped Conductive Polypyrrole:  Biomimetic Conducting Polymer for Cell Scaffolds and Electrodes

abstract: numerous regenerating tissues respond favorably to electrical stimulation, creating a need for a bioactive conducting platform for tissue engineering applications. the drive for biosensors and electrode coatings further requires control of the surface properties of promising conductive materials such as polypyrrole. here we present carboxy-endcapped polypyrrole (ppy-alpha-cooh), a unique bioactive conducting polymer with a carboxylic acid layer, composed of a polypyrrole (ppy) surface modified with pyrrole-alpha-carboxylic acid (py-alpha-cooh). this unique structure is simple to produce, provides a stable bioactive surface via covalent bonds, and preserves bulk properties such as electrical conductivity and mechanical integrity. the chemical structure of this polymer composite was characterized by angle-resolved x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (xps), which demonstrated the presence of carboxylic acid functionality on the top surface of conductive ppy. a four-point probe test was used to verify the similar conductivity of ppy-alpha-cooh compared to that of standard ppy. to demonstrate the potential to influence cellular activity, the carboxylic acid monolayer surface was grafted with the cell-adhesive arg-gly-asp (rgd) motif. human umbilical vein endothelial cells (huvecs) cultured on rgd-modified ppy-alpha-cooh demonstrated significantly higher adhesion and spreading than on the negative controls ppy-alpha-cooh and unmodified ppy.

title: hybrid acoustic metamaterial as super absorber for broadband low-frequency sound
display_name: Hybrid acoustic metamaterial as super absorber for broadband low-frequency sound
abstract: abstract a hybrid acoustic metamaterial is proposed as a new class of sound absorber, which exhibits superior broadband low-frequency sound absorption as well as excellent mechanical stiffness/strength. based on the honeycomb-corrugation hybrid core (h-c hybrid core), we introduce perforations on both top facesheet and corrugation, forming perforated honeycomb-corrugation hybrid (phch) to gain super broadband low-frequency sound absorption. applying the theory of micro-perforated panel (mpp), we establish a theoretical method to calculate the sound absorption coefficient of this new kind of metamaterial. perfect sound absorption is found at just a few hundreds hertz with two-octave 0.5 absorption bandwidth. to verify this model, a finite element model is developed to calculate the absorption coefficient and analyze the viscous-thermal energy dissipation. it is found that viscous energy dissipation at perforation regions dominates the total energy consumed. this new kind of acoustic metamaterials show promising engineering applications, which can serve as multiple functional materials with extraordinary low-frequency sound absorption, excellent stiffness/strength and impact energy absorption.

title: capturing heterogeneity in gene expression studies by surrogate variable analysis
display_name: Capturing Heterogeneity in Gene Expression Studies by Surrogate Variable Analysis
abstract: it has unambiguously been shown that genetic, environmental, demographic, and technical factors may have substantial effects on gene expression levels. in addition to the measured variable(s) of interest, there will tend to be sources of signal due to factors that are unknown, unmeasured, or too complicated to capture through simple models. we show that failing to incorporate these sources of heterogeneity into an analysis can have widespread and detrimental effects on the study. not only can this reduce power or induce unwanted dependence across genes, but it can also introduce sources of spurious signal to many genes. this phenomenon is true even for well-designed, randomized studies. we introduce "surrogate variable analysis" (sva) to overcome the problems caused by heterogeneity in expression studies. sva can be applied in conjunction with standard analysis techniques to accurately capture the relationship between expression and any modeled variables of interest. we apply sva to disease class, time course, and genetics of gene expression studies. we show that sva increases the biological accuracy and reproducibility of analyses in genome-wide expression studies.

title: nanomedicine: reshaping clinical practice
display_name: Nanomedicine: reshaping clinical practice
abstract: " for i was never so small as this before, never!" lewis carroll, alice's adventures in wonderland (1865) the 6th key symposium on nanomedicine was held in stockholm, sweden on september 9 11, 2009. the symposium featured presentations from numerous leading scientists in the field and was divided into four sessions, reflecting some of the principal areas of research in nanomedicine, i.e., regenerative medicine, drug delivery, imaging and diagnostics, and finally, toxicology and risk assessment. this review aims to convey the excitement that was evident at this event and also to summarize some of the key messages. in addition, in the current volume of the journal of internal medicine, several of the speakers at the symposium have provided state-of-the-art reviews of specific areas of research on the application of nanotechnologies in medicine (nanomedicine) and/or on potential adverse effects of engineered nanomaterials (nanotoxicology). there has been considerable progress in recent years in the field of regenerative medicine due to the emergence of nanotechnology and specifically as a result of the use of nano-textured surfaces or topographies to facilitate biomimetic tissue engineering. in his keynote lecture, dr. teruo okano (tokyo woman's medical university) discussed a method of 'cell sheet engineering' for scaffoldless tissue engineering, based on an innovative polymer-based technology, and its potential application in a variety of clinical conditions. using temperature-responsive culture surfaces of poly(n-isopropylacrylamide), cells can be harvested as a contiguous sheet of cells with an intact extracellular matrix and thick tissues are constructed by layering of these cell sheets in an iterative process [1]. transplantation of such cell sheets onto damaged hearts improved heart function in animal models, and evidence was also presented for beneficial clinical outcome in a patient suffering from dilated cardiomyopathy. in addition, dr. okano reported that clinical trials have been initiated for the assessment of cell sheet engineering of ocular cell sheets for the improvement of visual acuity of patients with corneal stem cell deficiencies. dr. cato laurencin (university of connecticut) discussed recent advances in the fabrication of nanostructured scaffolds from polymeric and composite materials for musculoskeletal tissue regeneration. these important studies are beginning to unravel how molecular cues that occur as nanoscale structures interact with cells and open up opportunities to modulate such cues to improve the regeneration of damaged tissue. nanofibers mimicking the structure of natural extracellular matrix are generated by a process of electrospinning of polymers, and elegant studies in which this technology was applied to the repair of tendons and the generation of bone were presented. in addition, 3d porous scaffolds have been shown to support the growth of genetically engineered stromal cells for sustained release of endothelial growth factors that promote vascularization [2]. in a similar vein, dr. j ns hilborn (uppsala university) presented promising preclinical studies on a new hyaluronan-based carrier for the osteoinductive growth factor, bone morphogenetic protein-2 (bmp-2), that has been shown to function as an injectable replacement for bone grafts in animal experiments. dr. samuel stupp (northwestern university) presented recent work on the development of a broad class of amphiphilic molecules that are programmed to self-assemble into nanoscale filaments with the capacity to display signals to cells and bind specific proteins or dna [3]. these nanostructures have been developed for a number of biological targets and clinical conditions, including repair and regeneration of neurons, angiogenesis, as well as bone and cartilage regeneration. in a recently published preclinical study, remarkable efficiency in functional recovery after spinal cord injury was demonstrated. treatment with peptide amphiphile (pa) molecules that self-assemble in vivo into supramolecular nanofibers resulted in the regeneration of both descending motor fibres and ascending sensory fibres through the lesion site in a clip compression model of spinal cord injury in mice. treatment with the pa also resulted in significant behavioural improvement. dr. joakim spatz (max-planck-institute for metals research) explored the concept of artificial engineering of cellular responses based on the use of an inorganic or polymeric support, patterned with specific signalling molecules in well-defined nanoscopic geometries. examples of environmental sensing resulting from the crosstalk between the assembly of dynamic actin-integrin links known as focal adhesions and the forces that come into play in the associated cytoskeletal network owing to actin polymerization and actomyosin contraction were presented. a deeper understanding of how cells sense their environment could suggest new strategies in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine. the application of nanotechnology to drug delivery is expected to have considerable impact on the pharmaceutical and biotechnological industries. the first lecture in the session on drug delivery was delivered by dr. robert langer (massachusetts institute of technology) who presented early work on tumour angiogenesis and the application of the so-called rabbit corneal pocket assay for monitoring of neovascular growth in live animals. the latter assay was instrumental for the discovery and purification of angiogenesis-regulatory molecules. he then focused on the issue of gene therapy and prefaced this discussion by citing the words of dr. inder verma, a leading authority on the development of viruses as gene therapy vectors, who famously said that 'there are only three problems in gene therapy: delivery, delivery, and delivery'. viral vectors are efficient but they pose safety concerns. synthetic vectors are potentially safer, cheaper and easier to produce, yet they are currently less efficient. however, recent studies have shown that lipid-like materials designated as 'lipidoids' that have been identified by high-throughput screening approaches outperform other commonly used transfection reagents and thus show promise for delivery of rna interference (rnai) therapeutics [4]. dr. gabriel lopez-berestein (university of texas md anderson cancer centre) discussed exciting new developments in sirna technology for cancer therapy [5]. one of the main challenges is to develop safe and effective carriers for systemic administration of sirnas, and dr. lopez-berestein described recent studies focusing on cationic liposomes as nanocarriers of sirna. promising results from animal models of ovarian cancer were presented. it was also noted that the expression of dicer and drosha, components of the cellular rna interference machinery, varies in specimens of ovarian cancer in patients, and, moreover, that the levels of dicer and drosha mrna in ovarian cancer cells have associations with outcomes. these observations highlight the need for 'personalized medicine' and this was indeed one of the common themes of this symposium. in a sense, the era of nanomedicine can be viewed as the era of personalized medicine [6]. multi-functional nanocarriers for combined therapeutic and diagnostic purposes are currently being developed in research laboratories (fig. 1). dr. naomi halas (rice university) explored the opportunities for cancer treatment without the use of a conventional, pharmaceutical drug. in this paradigm, nanosized gold shells (hollow or core-shell structures) serve as light-scattering beacons and impart highly effective therapeutic responses via their unparalleled light-to-heat conversion properties. the latter effect has been employed to induce cell death and tumour regression in various animal models, and the same concept is now being evaluated in clinical trials [7]. importantly, this nanoparticle platform for thermal ablation of tumours can be combined with magnetic resonance imaging (mri) contrast agents for the enhancement of simultaneous imaging modalities. multi-functional nanoparticles for drug delivery. schematic of a multi-functional nanocarrier that combines a specific targeting agent (usually an antibody or peptide) with nanoparticles for imaging (such as semiconductor nanoparticles/quantum dots or magnetic nanoparticles), a cell-penetrating agent, a stimulus-sensitive element for drug release, a stabilizing polymer to ensure biocompatibility (commonly polyethylene glycol) and the therapeutic compound(s) of interest. reprinted from [18] with permission from elsevier. dr. ruth duncan (cardiff university), one of the pioneers in research on polymer therapeutics, addressed the question as to where we are on the road to clinical application of nanomedicine. there is growing optimism that ever more sophisticated polymer-based vectors will be a significant addition to the armamentarium currently used for cancer therapy [8]. however, future success will depend on the choice of an appropriate (nontoxic) polymer in relation to its proposed use and route of administration, the rational design of new drugs and drug carriers, and improved analytical techniques for measuring polymer characteristics. in addition, an improved, quantitative understanding of pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics is also needed to bridge the gap between the bench and the clinic. there has been an increasing interest in ordered mesoporous silica matrices for biomedical applications. indeed, the combination of properties of these mesoporous materials such as high surface areas, and their textural properties, especially the well-ordered pore geometries, make these materials attractive for a variety of applications. dr. maria vallet-regi (the complutense university of madrid) provided exciting glimpses of recent studies on nanostructured mesoporous silica for regeneration of bone tissue and as drug delivery systems [9]. dr. alexander kabanov (university of nebraska) discussed polymeric micelles structures self-assembled from amphiphilic block copolymers containing hydrophilic and hydrophobic components. such structures form nanosized (10 100 nm) core-shell structures. drug molecules can be incorporated into the cores of the micelles and polymeric micellar drug formulations are currently undergoing clinical trials for treatment of cancer and other diseases. dr. kabanov presented remarkable results on such micelles with 'phenotypic selectivity' in which micelles loaded with cytotoxic drug are toxic to cancer cells and sensitize multi-drug resistant tumour cells, whilst sparing normal cells that do not internalize the micelles because of differences in their endocytic machineries. phase iii clinical trials of such block copolymers for treatment of oesophageal cancer are in progress. dr. vladimir torchilin (northeastern university) focused on the application of nanocarriers for delivery of 'undeliverable' drugs, i.e. drugs with poor solubility, low stability and rapid clearance from systemic circulation. more than half of all drug candidates are abandoned due to poor solubility and hence cannot be delivered as therapeutics. however, by applying layer-by-layer technology (alternate coating of nanoparticles of poorly soluble drugs with layers of oppositely charged biocompatible soluble polymers), stable nanocolloidal formulations of drugs can be prepared. dr. torchilin illustrated this concept with data on the preparation of paclitaxel-loaded 'immuno-micelles' bearing anti-tumour antibodies which were shown to accumulate in vivo in a lung carcinoma model in mice resulting in efficient inhibition of tumour growth [10]. the ability to measure and visualize proteins and their patterns of interactions and modifications is of key importance in basic science and in medicine, as this can afford new insights into cellular processes and their perturbation in disease. in his lecture, dr. ulf landegren (uppsala university) delved into the cellular proteome and presented a technology known as proximity ligation assay (pla) that harnesses dna for construction of protein assays of considerable specificity and sensitivity. examples of pla-based detection of disease markers and of viral proteins were given, including results from a recently published study on the detection of avian influenza virus, demonstrating that pla is nearly as sensitive as a commonly used real-time pcr assay, and much more sensitive than a conventional sandwich elisa, utilizing the same antibody. dr. charles lieber (harvard university) presented a visionary lecture on nanowire electronic devices and their potential application for ultrasensitive, multiplexed, label-free detection of disease markers [11]. importantly, because the sizes of biological macromolecules are comparable to nanowire building blocks, these structures represent natural transducers for detection in the size-range of biological systems. dr. lieber reported on the feasibility of detection of cancer markers at femtomolar concentrations in biological samples using silicon-nanowire field-effect devices. in addition, more recent studies have demonstrated that nanowire transistor arrays can be interfaced with specific regions of acute brain slices of the olfactory bulb to detect localized neuronal activities with very high resolution, and that these devices can also be employed to record electrical activity in embryonic chicken cardiomyocytes with high sensitivity. together, these studies suggest that research at the interface between engineered nanosystems and endogenous biosystems may yield important advances in diagnostics and clinical medicine. dr. sunney xie (harvard university) presented fascinating data on new imaging techniques for the visualization of biochemical processes. imaging of single fluorescent proteins with millisecond time resolution and nanometer spatial precision have thus been developed. such technologies may yield insights into the mechanisms of many processes in molecular biology, such as dna protein interactions, gene regulation, transcription, translation and replication. in addition, sensitive, label-free imaging techniques based on stimulated raman scattering microscopy for small drugs or metabolites [12], and stimulated emission microscopy for chromophores such as hemeproteins with undetectable fluorescence were discussed. these imaging modalities offer exciting possibilities for biomedicine. dr. hjalmar brismar (royal institute of technology) discussed techniques for studies of protein mobility using quantum dot-based single particle tracking. quantum dots (inorganic semiconductor nanocrystals) are well-suited for single particle tracking as they are photostable, thus permitting long exposure times/time-lapse recordings under the microscope. dr. chad mirkin (northwestern university) discussed polyvalent nucleic acid nano-conjugates and explored how these constructs can be utilized in biodiagnostics and for regulation of gene expression. it was noted that the application of dna nanoparticle (e.g. gold nanoparticle) conjugates in biodetection has the potential to challenge the medical community to move diagnostic tests from centralized laboratories to the point-of-care as these novel and sensitive methods allow for miniaturization of the test platform; indeed, us food and drug administration (fda)-approved tests are available for the in vitro diagnosis of several diseases including cystic fibrosis and blood coagulation disorders. one of the most significant obstacles for systemic delivery of payloads (drugs, nucleic acids) using nanocarriers is the foreign particle clearance by the mononuclear phagocyte system. the rate and extent of removal is determined by the physico-chemical properties of the materials used. dr. martin philbert (university of michigan) discussed strategies for evasion of macrophage clearance by the use of degradable polyacrylamide-based hydrogels. to avoid the accumulation of polyacrylamide-based nanoparticles in the body, short chain polyacrylamides were assembled into nanoparticles with degradable cross-linkers. these payloads are stable in aqueous environments but they quickly disintegrate under cytoplasmic conditions so as to release drugs once they enter cells. the development of biodegradable polymers may significantly reduce the toxicity of the nanocarrier. sustainable development of the nanotechnologies for use in the clinic will necessitate close attention to safety issues [13]. dr. g nter oberd rster (university of rochester) outlined basic concepts guiding nanotoxicological research, including the significance of dose, and the importance of a thorough understanding of physico-chemical properties of nanoparticles [14]. dr. oberd rster also presented recent data from animal studies of gold nanoparticles of different sizes in which the importance of the route of administration (intravenous injection versus inhalation) and the influence of particle coating/surface modification for biodistribution of particles were assessed. numerous challenges remain in nanotoxicological research: assessment of human and environmental exposure, identification of potential hazards of engineered nanomaterials, and the issue of biopersistence in tissues all need to be taken into account to perform meaningful risk assessment. the question as to whether nanoparticles can cross biological barriers and accumulate in secondary target organs following, for instance, inhalation has been debated in recent years. dr. wolfgang kreyling (german research centre for environmental health) presented interesting quantitative data on the accumulation of small fractions of nanoparticles (iridium, carbon, gold, titanium dioxide) in all secondary organs studied including the brain, heart and even in foetuses. the fractions were generally low but this depended strongly on particle size and surface modifications of the particles and on the route of administration. dr. kreyling concluded that it is possible that chronic exposure to nanoparticles may lead to accumulation in secondary organs at levels that are sufficient to induce adverse health effects. however, long-term exposure studies have yet to be conducted. dr. anna shvedova (national institute for occupational safety and health) focused her presentation on studies of single-walled carbon nanotubes (swcnt), which are common in a wide range of different technological applications and are also being considered for biomedical applications, including as vectors for delivery of drugs or nucleic acids. recent in vivo studies have shown that swcnt can elicit strong inflammatory and early-onset fibrogenic responses coupled with the induction of oxidative stress in the lung of mice exposed via pharyngeal aspiration or inhalation [15]. these effects occurred at doses of potential relevance to occupational scenarios. considerable attention has been drawn to the potential similarities between carbon nanotubes and asbestos fibres. dr. shvedova reported that inhalation of swcnt resulted in the occurrence of mutations in the k-ras oncogene in mice. moreover, in vitro studies conducted in primary human bronchial epithelial cells demonstrated that swcnt cause frequent disruption of cell division due to interference with the mitotic spindle. however, long-term studies are needed to assess whether these alterations will result in the formation of tumours of the lung or mesothelium. swcnt are considered to be highly biopersistent and are not readily recognized or engulfed by macrophages in the absence of specific surface modifications of these materials. dr. valerian kagan (university of pittsburgh) presented exciting data on the enzymatic biodegradation in vitro of swcnt in human neutrophils, key players of the innate immune system. biodegradation was accomplished through enzymatic catalysis by human neutrophil-derived myeloperoxidase (hmpo). functionalization of swcnt with immunoglobulin (igg) promoted cellular internalization of swcnt and enhanced the hmpo-dependent biodegradation. importantly, using an established model of pharyngeal aspiration of swcnt, it was shown that biodegradation of swcnt in vitro nullified their propensity to induce pulmonary inflammation and fibrosis. these findings indicate that biomedical applications of cnts may be achievable under conditions of carefully controlled biodegradation. when nanoparticles are introduced into the body, intentionally or unintentionally, what do cells really see? dr. kenneth dawson (university college dublin) discussed this important aspect of nanomedicine/nanotoxicology, and introduced the concept of a protein 'corona' that results from a dynamic exchange of proteins and lipids between the surface of nanoparticles and environment [16]. the exchange rates are sometimes so slow that many biological responses are likely defined by these associated biomolecules. it follows from this argument that it is of crucial importance to develop methods to study the identity of title: effect of design parameters on the cushioning property of cellular fabric composites
display_name: Effect of design parameters on the cushioning property of cellular fabric composites
abstract: in this study, a new design method for a three-dimensional hollow structure woven fabric was proposed and the effect of cellular size on the cushioning property of the fabric-reinforced polyurethane elastomer composite was investigated. the fabric structure was analyzed from a cross-section view and the theoretical equations for the warp and weft yarns were proposed, using the fabric layer and cellular size as parameters. nine kinds of fabrics with different layers and cellular size were fabricated with a jacquard loom and reinforced with polyurethane elastomer to yield fabric composites. then the effect of cellular size on the cushioning property of the fabric composites was discussed. the results showed that upon increasing the cellular size, the cellular fabric composite exhibited lower compression resistance. moreover, the stress at a strain of 65% and the energy absorbed in the loading process were increased with decreasing cellular size. moreover, the compression resilience was also changed with the cellular size. it can be concluded that the cellular size had an important effect on the cushioning property of the fabric composite, which can be considered as a design parameter for cushion material based on its usages.

title: pluronic block-copolymers in medicine: from chemical and biological versatility to rationalisation and clinical advances
display_name: Pluronic® block-copolymers in medicine: from chemical and biological versatility to rationalisation and clinical advances
abstract: this mini-review highlights the latest advances in the chemistry and biology of pluronic triblock copolymers. we focus on their applications in medicine, as drug delivery carriers, biological response modifiers, and pharmaceutical ingredients. examples of drug delivery systems and formulations currently in clinical use, clinical trials or preclinical development are highlighted. we also discuss the role that pluronic copolymers may play in the innovative design of new nanomedicines in the near future.

title: artificial brownian motors: controlling transport on the nanoscale
display_name: Artificial Brownian motors: Controlling transport on the nanoscale
abstract: in systems possessing spatial or dynamical symmetry breaking, brownian motion combined with unbiased external input signals, deterministic and random alike, can assist directed motion of particles at submicron scales. in such cases, one speaks of ``brownian motors.{''} in this review the constructive role of brownian motion is exemplified for various physical and technological setups, which are inspired by the cellular molecular machinery: the working principles and characteristics of stylized devices are discussed to show how fluctuations, either thermal or extrinsic, can be used to control diffusive particle transport. recent experimental demonstrations of this concept are surveyed with particular attention to transport in artificial, i.e., nonbiological, nanopores, lithographic tracks, and optical traps, where single-particle currents were first measured. much emphasis is given to two- and three-dimensional devices containing many interacting particles of one or more species; for this class of artificial motors, noise rectification results also from the interplay of particle brownian motion and geometric constraints. recently, selective control and optimization of the transport of interacting colloidal particles and magnetic vortices have been successfully achieved, thus leading to the new generation of microfluidic and superconducting devices presented here. the field has recently been enriched with impressive experimental achievements in building artificial brownian motor devices that even operate within the quantum domain by harvesting quantum brownian motion. sundry akin topics include activities aimed at noise-assisted shuttling other degrees of freedom such as charge, spin, or even heat and the assembly of chemical synthetic molecular motors. this review ends with a perspective for future pathways and potential new applications.

title: strong and durable wood designed by cell wall bulking combined with cell lumen filling
display_name: Strong and Durable Wood Designed by Cell Wall Bulking Combined with Cell Lumen Filling
abstract: traditional wood polymer composite (wpc) based on the in situ polymerization of ethylene unsaturated monomers in the cellular cavity of wood is significant for the high-value-added utilization of low-quality wood. however, this type of wpc has the problems of volatile monomers, low conversion rates, odor residue, and poor compatibility between the polymer and wood interface, which hinder its promotion and application. in this study, a two-step process of cell wall bulking in combination with cell lumen filling was prepared to modify wood using maleic anhydride (man) as the bulking agent and gma-egdma (molar ratio 2:1) as the active monomer system. the results indicate that the modulus of rupture (mor) (125.19 8.41 mpa), compressive strength (116.38 7.69 mpa), impact toughness (55.4 2.95 kj m 2), and hardness (6187 273 n) of the bulking filling wood composite materials were improved by 54%, 56%, 36%, and 66%, respectively, compared with those of poplar wood. these properties were superior to those of the traditional styrene (pst)-wpc and even exceeded the performance of xylosma congesta (lour.) merr, a high-quality wood from northeast china. meanwhile, the mass loss of wood composite materials with bulking filling treatment was only 2.35 0.05%, and the internal structure remained intact, presenting excellent decay resistance. additionally, the treatment also significantly improved the thermal and dimensional stability of the wood composites. this study provides a theoretical basis and guidance for realizing the high-value-added application of low-quality wood and the preparation of highly durable wood-based composites.

title: biocompatible probes based on rare-earth doped strontium aluminates with long-lasting phosphorescent properties for in vitro optical imaging
display_name: Biocompatible Probes Based on Rare-Earth Doped Strontium Aluminates with Long-Lasting Phosphorescent Properties for In Vitro Optical IMAGING
abstract: in recent decades, the demand for biomedical imaging tools has grown very rapidly as a key feature for biomedical research and diagnostic applications. particularly, fluorescence imaging has gained increased attention as a non-invasive, inexpensive technique that allows real-time imaging. however, tissue auto-fluorescence under external illumination, together with a weak tissue penetration of low wavelength excitation light, largely restricts the application of the technique. accordingly, new types of fluorescent labels are currently being investigated and, in this search, phosphorescent nanoparticles promise great potential, as they combine the interesting size-dependent properties of nanoscale materials with a long-lasting phosphorescence-type emission that allows optical imaging well after excitation (so avoiding autofluorescence). in this work, core-shell structures consisting of sralo:eu,dy luminescent cores encapsulated within a biocompatible silica shell were prepared, showing a green persistent phosphorescence with an afterglow time of more than 1000 s. a high-energy ball milling procedure was used to reduce the size of the starting phosphors to a size suitable for cellular uptake, while the silica coating was produced by a reverse micelle methodology that eventually allows the excitation and emission light to pass efficiently through the shell. confocal fluorescence microscopy using hela cancer cells confirmed the potential of the all-ceramic composites produced as feasible labels for in vitro optical imaging.

abstract: abstract metal-organic frameworks (mofs) with high porosity and designable functionality make it possible to access the merits of high permeability and selectivity. however, scalable fabrication methods to produce mixed matrix membranes (mmms) with good flexibility and ultrahigh mof loading are urgently needed yet largely unmet. herein, we report a thermally induced phase separation-hot pressing (tips-hop) strategy to roll-to-roll produce 10 distinct mof-membranes (loadings up to 86 wt%). ultrahigh-molecular-weight polyethylene interweaving the mof particles contributes to their mechanical strength. rejections (99%) of organic dyes with a water flux of 125.7 l m 2 h 1 bar 1 under cross-flow filtration mode. the micron-sized channels between the mof particles translate into fast water permeation, while the porous mofs reject solutes through rapid adsorption. this strategy paves ways for developing high-performance membrane adsorbers for crucial separation processes. as a proof-of-concept, the abilities of the membrane adsorbers for separating racemates and proteins have been demonstrated.

abstract: abstract tissue engineering repair of annulus fibrosus (af) defects has the potential to prevent disability and pain from intervertebral disc (ivd) herniation and its progression to degeneration. clinical translation of af repair methods requires assessment in long term large animal models. an ovine af injury model was developed using cervical spinal levels and a biopsy type af defect to assess composite tissue engineering repair in 1 month and 12 month studies. the repair used a fibrin hydrogel crosslinked with genipin (fibgen) to seal defects, poly(trimethylene carbonate) (ptmc) scaffolds to replace lost af tissue, and polyurethane membranes to prevent herniation. in the 1 month study, ptmc scaffolds sealed with fibgen herniated with polyurethane membranes. when applied alone, fibgen integrated with the surrounding af tissue without herniation, showing promise for long term studies. the 12 month long term study used only fibgen which showed fibrous healing, biomaterial resorption and no obvious hydrogel related complications. however, the 2 mm biopsy punch injury condition also exhibited fibrotic healing at 12 months. both untreated and fibgen treated groups showed equivalency with no detectable differences in histological grades of proteoglycans, cellular morphology, ivd structure and blood vessel formation, biomechanical properties including torque range and axial range of motion, pfirrmann grade, ivd height, and quantitative scores of vertebral body changes from clinical computed tomography. the biopsy type injury caused endplate defects with a high prevalence of osteophytes in all groups and no nucleus herniation, indicating that the biopsy type injury requires further refinement, such as reduction to a slit type defect that could penetrate the full depth of the af without damaging the endplate. results demonstrate translational feasibility of fibgen for af repair to seal af defects, although future study with a more refined injury model is required to validate the efficacy of fibgen before translation.

abstract: a re-entrant honeycomb structure made from a novel solid composite based on recycled rubber is an innovative and sustainable solution for engineering applications. this work describes the tensile and failure behaviour of multi re-entrant honeycomb topologies consisting of width, thickness and angle variations. finite element (fe) models were also developed to simulate tensile tests and failure behaviour of the cellular structures. a taguchi design (l8) was conducted to determine the effect of each factor on the ultimate strength, ultimate strain, modulus of elasticity, poisson's ratio and von mises stress. the experimental and fe results showed a good correlation, validating the numerical model which was used to perform a parametric analysis on the influence of the cell geometry over the failure behaviour of the structures. the magnitude of poisson's ratio was significantly affected by the level of each cell geometric parameter. the structures with lower poisson's ratio values were able to absorb more energy, and consequently, exhibiting less points of failure. it was found the thickness and the width has a significant effect on the tensile properties and failure behaviour.

title: electrospun titania fiber mats spin coated with thin polymer films as nanofibrous scaffolds for enhanced cell proliferation
display_name: Electrospun titania fiber mats spin coated with thin polymer films as nanofibrous scaffolds for enhanced cell proliferation

abstract: the incorporation of inorganic materials into electrospun nanofibres has recently gained considerable attention for the development of extracellular matrix-like scaffolds with improved mechanical properties and enhanced biological functions for tissue engineering applications. in this study, polymer-inorganic composite fibres consisting of poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) (peoxa) and tetrabutyl titanate as the titanium precursor were successfully fabricated through a combined sol-gel/electrospinning approach. peoxa/ti(or) n composite fibres were obtained with varying amounts of polymer and titanium precursors. calcinations of the composite fibres were performed at varying temperatures to produce tio 2 fibres (tio 2 -t-60) with anatase, anatase/rutile mixed phase, and rutile crystal structures. thin polymer films (i.e., poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) (peoxa), polycaprolactone (pcl), and poly(methyl methacrylate) (pmma)) were subsequently deposited onto tio 2 -t-60 fibre mats by spin coating to facilitate handling of the electrospun substrates after calcination, which are rather brittle and disintegrate easily, and to probe cell-materials interactions. the cellular behaviour of mouse l929 fibroblasts after culture periods of 1-5 days was compared on the following fibre scaffolds: peoxa/ti(or) n , tio 2 -t-60 (t = 600, 650, and 700 c), tio 2 -t-60 spin-coated with thin pcl film (pcl/tio 2 -t-60), and pure pcl. the results obtained from in vitro cell culture studies for the lactate dehydrogenase release assay and confocal microscopic visualization pointed out the synergistic interplay between the tio 2 crystal structure and spin-coated pcl film in facilitating cell interactions with the scaffold surface. the l929 cells were observed to adhere and proliferate better on the surface of tio 2 -700-60 having the rutile structure than on the surfaces of tio 2 -600-60 and tio 2 -650-60 fibre scaffolds with anatase and anatase/rutile mixed phase structures, respectively.
